I am seventy-one years old, and I have farmed the flat land of Quzhou County since I was a young man. I never went to school, but I know this soil and this climate with my hands and my eyes. My family has about six mu of good irrigated land, and I do not plan to change what has worked for generations.

The wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October after the autumn rains, using an improved *lumai* variety from the local seed station. Now that spring has arrived, my first job is to topdress it with nitrogen when the wheat turns green, irrigate it from my well, and spray for weeds. I will irrigate three times in total: at green-up, at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once more when the ears are filling. I use rotary tillage for the wheat seedbed because it breaks up the stubble and prepares a fine bed for sowing. I will spray herbicide once in early spring, and if aphids or rust appear, I will add insecticide and fungicide — about three sprayings in total. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer as a base and then topdress with urea. I expect around 950 jin of wheat per mu.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant summer maize the same week. There is no time to waste between the two crops, so I sow directly into the wheat stubble without tillage — everyone here does it this way now, and the machines can drill the seeds right in. I use hybrid seeds, usually *Denghai* or *Nongda* varieties, because they grow fast and yield well. I put compound fertilizer in the row at sowing, and that is usually enough phosphorus and potassium for the season. Maize needs less water than wheat, so I irrigate twice: once when it is knee-high and again when the tassels come out. I control weeds early and watch for corn borers, so I plan about three pesticide applications. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 1,050 jin of grain per mu.

I do not grow cotton or vegetables anymore — at my age, I cannot manage the extra labor, and the wheat-maize rotation gives me steady food and income with work I can still handle, especially when my family helps with the harvest.

decision.reasoning_summary: I have farmed in Quzhou County for over fifty years on six mu of irrigated land. The wheat-maize double-cropping system is the only sensible use of this soil and climate, and it is what I know. Winter wheat is already sown in autumn; I now manage it through spring with topdressing, three irrigations, and weed and pest control, using rotary tillage for the seedbed. After harvest in early June, I immediately sow hybrid summer maize with no-tillage to save time and labor, applying basal compound fertilizer and irrigating twice. At seventy-one, I avoid crops that demand heavy or unpredictable labor, relying instead on the stable rotation that has fed my family for decades.
